An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time interval has been made using $7.8$ inverse picobarns of LHCb data from $5.0$ teravolt protons colliding $25$ billion times. This measure was obtained with no notable discrepancies found in various bin sizes, and the outcomes from different analytical methods conformed to the $B^0_s$ oscillation frequency expected in the Standard Model. The most precise outcome yielded a measure of $4.4\times 10^{-8}$ seconds with a $95\%$ confidence level. This measure serves as the primary restriction for searching $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay with violation of $CP$ symmetry at future more powerful colliders. The most limiting factor in this study was the uncertainty in measuring the decay time interval, and further improvement in LHCb data or with the LHC's upgraded detector is expected to achieve a time interval sensitivity ten times more precise by $13$-by$29$ range. The method employed in this measurement also enabled calculation of $B^0_s\rightarrow $\pi^+\pi^-$ decay time interval, resulting in a more precise $4.9\times 10^{-8}$ seconds. This study was carried out in conjunction with other analyses using the same data set. The outcome of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time interval measurement has been used to control for a bias that could influence the measurement of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time interval and the presence rate of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay with violation of $CP$ symmetry. The presence rate of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay with violation of $CP$ symmetry was found to be below the standard model expected rate with a $95\%$ confidence level in all bin sizes and analytical methods used, and the outcome from different analytical methods conformed to the $B^0_s$ oscillation frequency expected in the Standard Model. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals an apparent correlation with the distribution of nearby galaxies. At energies exceeding 4 x 10^18 eV, the cosmic rays show a significant anisotropy, with a 3.6 sigma confidence level. We observed a concentration of cosmic rays towards a region containing 16% more galaxies than would be expected by chance, specifically in the direction of the Cetus-Draco complex and surrounding areas. Furthermore, we found a smaller anisotropy with a 2.8 sigma confidence level towards a region containing 4% more galaxies than would be expected by chance, located at about 65 degrees across from the primary direction. These findings were consistent across different cosmic ray particle types. We estimated that approximately 3-4% of extremely energetic cosmic rays originate from sources within 100 million light-years. We also found that these sources emit cosmic rays with an anisotropic distribution, with up to 10% more likelihood towards the Cetus-Draco direction, and that they do so over a wide angle of approximately 45 degrees. We observed that the cosmic rays exhibit a preference for the southern hemisphere, and this preference becomes more pronounced at higher energies, although this preference does not significantly impact our findings. We considered various explanations for these findings, including the possibility that these sources are binary compact object mergers, active galactic nuclei, or starburst galaxies, and found that they cannot be ruled out based on the data presented here. Further study is needed to fully comprehend these findings and the nature of these sources. The methods and findings presented in this study could also provide a framework for interpreting the data that will be collected by the AugerPrime upgrade to the Pierre Auger Observatory and other extremely energetic cosmic ray detectors. In addition, the findings presented here could provide a better understanding of the universe above 4 x 10^18 eV, a region that was previously inaccessible until the detection of extremely energetic cosmic rays. The detection of these extremely energetic cosmic rays has significantly improved our understanding of the universe in this energy range, and will continue to do so with future studies. The findings presented in this study could also provide a better understanding of the production of extremely energetic cosmic rays, which could lead to a greater comprehension of the fundamental processes that govern the universe. In surgical pathology, tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are a significant factor in predicting patient outcomes and developing personalized treatment plans. Automated detection and categorization of TILs in surgical tissue samples can accelerate clinical diagnosis, but this process is complex and highly variable, depending on factors such as tissue sample quality, staining methods, and the presence of non-lymphocytic components. To address these challenges, a novel approach based on deep learning was developed to categorize TILs in H&E stained sections of metastatic breast cancer tissues. The approach involved two primary sub-tasks: 1) locating and outlining TIL regions, and 2) classifying non-melanotic TILs according to the frequency of cell nuclei within defined regions. This study demonstrates a federated learning technique to facilitate a collaborative environment among participating institutions, allowing for the development of a robust TIL categorization model without the exchange of sensitive clinical data. This method enables models to be trained on institutional datasets while minimizing the risk of data breaches and promoting diversity through collaborative learning. In this study, a federated approach was applied to a challenging clinical classification task involving over 28,000 images from 15 participating institutions. The results show that federated learning yields a reliable and efficient TIL categorization model, outperforming a baseline model developed using a non-federated approach. This method demonstrates a significant advantage in model performance, achieving a 6.3% reduction in loss error compared to the baseline model. This innovative approach to developing models from heterogeneous, distributed datasets has the potential to accelerate the development of efficient and robust clinical models for real-world applications. To further explore this method, the study provides a detailed analysis of the federated learning process and presents results from a qualitative assessment of the model's performance. This assessment includes a comparative evaluation of the model's predictions with expert annotations and the identification of institutional contributions to the model. This study can serve as a model for the development of robust, real-world clinical models through federated learning. During a field trial in a 4800km submarine fiber cable transmitting 43Gbit/s Nyquist-shaped signals, the proposed DFE receiver design showed a significant reduction in bit error rate (BER), successfully limiting BER below the forward error correction (FEC) threshold despite high ion dispersion and burst errors induced by deep fiber nonlinearity. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses solvability, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are nilpotent when the field in question is perfect. Our proof follows from a more general phenomenon, where we demonstrate that the combination of any nilpotent Lie algebra and the algebra's derived series results in a Zinbiel algebra, which is subsequently demonstrated to be finite-dimensional when combined with the Lie algebra. This combined algebra then inherits the property of nilpotency from its Lie algebra component. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the dimensions of these algebras. Furthermore, we offer a characterization of the simplest types of Zinbiel algebras, which includes their exponential and solvable forms, as well as a discussion on the variety they represent. Lastly, we provide a method for determining the solvability class of these algebras using their basis elements. This research is a follow-up to our earlier findings on nilpotent Zinbiel algebras, which can be found in our previous paper. This concept has been the basis for various works on modal logic through the application of dualities. In our research, we expand upon this concept, creating an inverse language that unifies Deductive, Equational, and PDL-Logics with Inverse. This combined language, which we call DLE-Inv, becomes the fundamental framework for our examination of inverse relations in logic. Through this framework, we explore the relationship between the semantics and the proof theory of DLE-Inv, demonstrating that the application of dualities results in a equivalent logic regarding both deduction and equivalence. Additionally, we investigate the connection between the pre-fix point operators and the Scott induction principle in the case of DLE-Inv. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of an inverse equivalence for a family of functions, which leads to a deeper understanding of the connection between the application of dualities and the translation of formulas. This results in an equivalent formulation of the translation of a formula into its'mirror image', which can be expressed using the syntax of the original logic. This expression, which we call the unified inverse, holds for any DLE-Logic. This unified inverse can be used to translate a formula and its counterpart into corresponding formulas of the underlying logic. This translation is then applied to the basic DLE-Logics, which includes the application of the unified inverse to the logic of positivity, the combination of core and extended positive modal logic, and the extension of basic distributive law with pre-fix points. This research also explores the extension of basic distributive law with a countable number of pre-fix points, which is a key contribution. This combined language, DLE-Inv, with a countable number of pre-fix points provides a universal framework for any DLE-Logic with a countable number of pre-fix points. This research provides the foundation for the exploration of rich modal logics that result from the application of dualities to the combination of core and extended positive modal logic. These exceptions can be used to manage tidiness during data integration, blending, and other operations that merge tables containing nulls and FDs. To facilitate this approach, we developed a novel way to represent a table as a set of exceptions and an expanded version of the data, along with an algorithm to achieve consistent interpretation. We also established bounds for the number of temporary exceptions that can be created and a strategy for updating tables with nulls and FDs. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. NDFs are created using a three-part system where a
descriptor network generates a global descriptor based on an object's overall
appearance, producing a descriptor that can identify the object's category.
Additionally, a mask network, fueled by 2D bounding boxes containing key object
points, extracts a descriptor that describes these specific points in 3D space.
Lastly, a score network, using a combination of the global and point descriptors,
predicts a probability score indicating how accurate the 3D pose reconstruction
is. We test NDFs on the ModelNet40 dataset, achieving exceptional results in
object instance recognition and pose estimation when cross-referencing 2D and 3D
descriptions, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. NDFs also
exhibit great performance in handling partial views, demonstrating robustness in
pose estimation. Furthermore, results show that NDFs can transfer knowledge from
one object category to another, showing great potential in applications where
there is limited labeling available. NDFs can be trained end-to-end using a
simple yet effective loss function comprising a triplet loss and a mask loss. A
mask loss is introduced to enhance the accuracy of point descriptors, achieving
this by matching a descriptor of a given 3D point against a set of descriptors
from a group of nearby points with the understanding that only one of these
points corresponds to the target 3D point. A key benefit of NDFs is that all
components of the system are equivariant to spatial transformations, ensuring
that the representation remains consistent with physical laws. A key drawback of
NDFs, however, is that they require a large amount of data to train. A major
limitation of NDFs is that they rely on the use of 3D bounding boxes containing
key object points, which can be difficult to obtain. Additionally, NDFs only
consider a single object at a time, making it not suitable for applications

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the SiD's robust design, only minor modifications are needed to significantly enhance the detector's capabilities, including the addition of a photon tracker and a more sophisticated trigger system. These enhancements aim to raise the detector's benchmark performance in certain areas to the level of the ILD concept, without compromising its inherent characteristics. The modified SiD detector will be presented, highlighting the underlying reasons for the changes and the underlying detector design principles. Furthermore, the implications of these modifications on the detector's operation and reconstruction methods will be discussed. Carrying out the study required obtaining high-resolution spectroscopy of the stars' spectra, which was achieved with the use of the CAPOS survey's integrated spectra of the cluster, combined with the addition of high signal-to-noise, high-resolution spectroscopy of the stars themselves. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes were first identified by Weisberg in 1971, but his study was conducted at relatively high speeds. In contrast, this research examines the splash dome closure in the middle speed range and reveals that the closure occurs before the sphere reaches the water's surface. Additionally, it was observed that the angle at which the sphere closes the water surface is nearly perpendicular in this intermediate speed range. This understanding of the surface seal regime may be useful in designing water-based shock absorbers and other technological applications. In computer systems, achieving hardware diversity involves using different hardware components to operate various functions. However, introducing new hardware also presents opportunities for malicious insertion, either physically or digitally. To address this issue, we need to develop a framework that evaluates and mitigates the risks associated with hardware manipulation across the system's software and hardware components. Our research identifies potential attacks on modern operating systems and proposes a framework, Hardware Trust Layer, to provide diverse hardware functionality while minimizing the reliance on hardware for specific operations. We demonstrate this framework's efficacy by creating a prototype for a range of hardware components, including CPUs, GPUs, network interfaces, and memory modules. Our results show that our framework can effectively reduce the threat of malicious hardware insertion by at least 7.5 times for CPU, 6.4 times for GPU, 5.7 times for network interface, and 5.2 times for memory module. We have also incorporated our approach into a research operating system and present our design and implementation strategy. Our research lays the groundwork for the development of secure systems that can tolerate malicious hardware and provides a framework for system designers to create secure system software and manage hardware trust. Durable and secure hardware components are provided through our hardware trust layer, which enables system software to be secure and reliable. Furthermore, our research facilitates the exploration of innovative hardware protection technologies and presents a new methodology for evaluating system software's hardware trust management. We have introduced a protocol for validating the credibility of hardware components and developed a tool to monitor and manage hardware trust, including the detection of malicious hardware components and promoting good citizenship among system software. Our research has been recognized and has inspired the development of the HTR (Hardware Trust Layer) research operating system. HTR is an open-source research project that focuses on providing diverse hardware functionality to operate-system software while minimizing reliance on hardware. HTR incorporates the hardware trust-layer framework and includes several innovative hardware-protection technologies and protocols for validating hardware credibility and detecting malicious hardware components. HTR also includes a hardware-trust management monitor and a good-citizen-encouragement module to promote good citizenship among system software. HTR is designed to address the challenge of malicious hardware insertion and provides a reliable and secure system for computer-system software. Additionally, HTR enables system software to achieve hardware diversity and provides a trustworthy hardware component for operating systems. Our research has also inspired several new research projects, including the exploration of innovative hardware-protection technologies and the development of secure system software. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by multiple phonons, alongside unprecedented multi-phonon coherences in this type of quantum acoustic resonator. Moreover, this improvement enables the creation of robust anti-phase states of matter composed of multiple phonons, and the implementation of phonon-based quantum information processing tasks, such as a phonon-controlled phase gate, all facilitated by an impervious coherence of a dark exciton state. The revised model also reveals that, over a broad range of laser powers, the fluctuations in the Rabi frequency can be extremely large, specifically exceeding the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and might be applicable in developing new precision measurement tools. Furthermore, this research is being led by young scientists at the Institute for Integrated Electrical Systems and Quantum research, University of Federal Square, Germany. The work described within this article has been financially supported by the DFG, the European Research Council, the Helmholtz Association, the Institute for Integrated Electrical Systems and Quantum research, and the University of Federal Square, Germany. Additionally, the theoretical model developed can be experimentally validated utilizing a combination of time and frequency domain spectroscopy, accompanied by a semiconductor quantum dot model validated through experimental data. The file name for the quantum circuit containing the time-domain experiment is provided within the supplementary materials. Furthermore, both bright and dark exciton states within the quantum dot model are subject to a rigorous open system analysis, and multiple phonon coherences can be achieved through a combination of a laser power and a coupling strength. We highlight the method's benefits, particularly in complex scenarios involving time-delayed and nonlinear systems. A case study is also included to illustrate the applicability of this approach, focusing on a ventilator system that can treat two COVID-19 patients sharing the same ventilation equipment. Due to the critical nature of medical ventilation, it is essential to ensure a high level of precision in the treatment. We demonstrate how the direct transcription approach can be applied to control the airflow, oxygen concentration, and pressure in this life-support system, which is prone to oscillations and other disturbances. We emphasize the computational advantages of this method over alternative predictive control systems, acknowledging the heightened risk aversion that is common in critical care applications. We conclude that the direct transcription approach is a reliable and efficient solution for complex control system design problems, and we anticipate that it will be of further utility in the development of life-support systems for the patients most severely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic and other respiratory diseases. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate a more straightforward approach to identify tumors in the esophagus by training a deep learning algorithm using sole reference to the CT scans. Our proposed algorithm, named Dilated Dense Focus Attention Unet, successfully detected and outlined tumors in the esophagus during a competition known as the Data Science Bowl 2017, and our results revealed that it outperformed several other entry submissions. Our research demonstrates the capability of a deep learning algorithm to accurately identify and outline tumors in the esophagus from CT scans without requiring additional information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated parsing process, using a singlearseor parser to generate all possible entity structures from the syntactic dependencies in the sentence. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset, called BiOME, which includes hierarchical annotations and offers a more comprehensive and realistic testing ground for nested NER models. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on BiOME and outperforms linear models on the AITE dataset. Moreover, we find that hierarchical modeling is essential for accurate nested entity extraction. Real-world datasets are typically assembled through crowdsourcing, involving both brief and detailed descriptions, which are compared to each other in terms of quality. It has been observed that these crowdsourced ratings often contradict expert opinions, which can result in uncomfortable consequences, such as unintentionally reinforcing discriminatory practices, when used to train models. Additionally, these datasets may not adequately reflect the capabilities of generated descriptions when compared to other evaluation metrics, such as measurement of generated text's similarity to human-generated descriptions. For these reasons, there is a growing interest in exploring alternative methods for evaluating image description generation that are less dependent on human-generated descriptions. MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging methods, such as contrast agents, can further enhance diagnostic accuracy by highlighting specific areas or functions within the body. To aid in the manual analysis of MRI scans by medical specialists, Computer-Assisted Diagnostic (CAD) systems have been developed, incorporating image processing algorithms to pinpoint specific features or abnormalities. These CAD systems have several key components, including image preprocessing modules that enhance image quality and retrieve vital medical information. To prepare images for subsequent processing and analysis, techniques like normalization, smoothing, and filtering are applied to the MRI scans. Once preprocessed, features are extracted using methods such as texture analysis, region of interest identification, and shape analysis, providing a numerical representation of the image that can be used for classification, segmentation, or other medical operations. After feature extraction, a classification or regression algorithm is applied to generate a numerical value or to classify the image into a particular category, respectively. This output is then compared to gold standard data, allowing for the evaluation of the system's performance and potential areas for improvement. To facilitate learning from multiple datasets, techniques like data fusion and merging have been developed. These methods, although effective in the medical field, also pose challenges related to the selection of appropriate algorithms, features, and parameters. This proposed methodology can be applied to a variety of medical applications, including the analysis of MRI scans. To demonstrate this method's effectiveness, a study was conducted on a dataset of MRI images containing tumors. The proposed system was developed using a combination of image processing techniques, feature extraction methods, and a classification algorithm. The system's performance was evaluated and compared to a previously reported study. Although the proposed system outperformed the benchmark, it failed to achieve the optimal results predicted by the proposed methodology. To improve the system's performance, a trial and error approach was employed, involving the optimization of algorithm parameters, the selection of alternative features, and the application of different classification methods. These modifications led to a significant improvement in the system's accuracy, but resulted in a higher computational time. This challenge cannot be overcome by standalone object detectors due to their limited ability to understand context across images. To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel approach that leverages semantic information from neighbouring frames to aid object detection in currently unseen images. To evaluate our proposed approach, we create a new dataset that comprises image sequences with no context shared among frames. This dataset serves as a platform to assess a deep object detector's capacity to learn from visual context across images. This training allows the model to learn fundamental properties of objects from start, thus we call it a 'bare' model. To validate our proposed approach, we compare the performance of the bare model and a model that is trained on our dataset consisting of image sequences, alongside the bare model. This comparison is carried out on a separate set of image sequences where ground truth information is available. Organ procurement agencies face the challenge of maximizing the number of successful kidney transplants from a limited supply of donated organs. This issue is particularly critical for incompatible patients on the waiting list. In this paper, we present a kidney allocation system that prioritizes patients based on their level of incompatibility with available donors. The system aims to minimize the number of patients who are unable to receive a transplant and is proven to achieve this optimal outcome. Furthermore, we analyze the extent to which patient compatibility restricts the allocation of kidneys. In addition, we provide a kidney allocation algorithm that considers multiple transplant centers and identify optimal acceptances for every patient on the waiting list. This framework can be applied to various incompatible kidney allocation problems. In partnership with UNOS, we utilize real-world data to illustrate the practical implications of our approach and reveal the magnitude of the challenge posed by patient incompatibility. Finally, we explore ways to further optimize the system through the acceptance of kidneys that are incompatible with more than one patient. In this expanded framework, we present an integer programming solution and validate its effectiveness with a smaller dataset. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this issue, we explore alternative deep learning approaches that are designed to unravel the embedding space and alleviate the entanglement of these distributions. Our experiments demonstrate the advantages of these models in improving the classification of text polarities, highlighting the significance of addressing the limitations of these models in complex and non-stationary datasets. Our study has important implications for any application relying on these models, and we emphasize the necessity of conducting thorough explicit analyses of the underlying statistical learning principles that these models employ. Our work also raises concerns about the reliance on these models for tasks that assume a deep understanding of the underlying syntax and semantics, highlighting the danger of over-interpreting their performances. Multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms rely on the assumption that agents can accurately observe each other's actions in a shared game. Yet, in situations where states and actions are complex and broadly observed, such as in epidemiology, economic systems, or electronic commerce, this assumption may no longer hold, and the need arises for more sophisticated models that can handle observation errors and misperceptions. The proposed ExiNEX algorithm addresses this challenge by incorporating axiomatic notions of equilibria into a context where agents make suboptimal decisions based on their observations of other agents' actions, and it achieves this by applying a new, generalized proof of the NEG learning result. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems, reinforcement learning algorithms utilize replay buffers to leverage past experiences. As the size of the buffer increases, the average reward estimates are normalized, reducing the impact of individual extreme values. This normalization has a profound effect, as the squared errors used in optimization become a function of the variance of the rewards. We explore a quantitative approach to minimize variance while scaling the replay buffer, resulting in a general framework that can be applied to various policy optimization methods. Our case studies demonstrate notable improvements in optimizing hyperparameters for both a simple gridworld and the ALE game collection. We found that our variance dimnished experience replay framework yields a 3.84% average speedup in optimization and increases the successful rate from 31% to 100% in game collection, achieving expert level performance on 5 out of 49 games. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hjdwang/vder. We also introduce an efficient way to sample diverse experiences and a mini-batch policy gradient algorithm that reduces computation time. Our approach accelerates the learning process and allows for larger memory sizes, allowing for the optimization of hyperparameters that further accelerate policy optimization. Effective quantum chromodynamics (QCD) predictions for differential distributions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) can be made for certain processes involving a single jet or a pair of jets by using precision parton distribution functions (PDFs). These predictions are accurate at next-to-leading order (NLO) and include the impact of heavy quarks in the range of masses relevant to the LHC, thanks to the inclusion of perturbative PDFs in the form of perturbative TMDs. In this paper, we examine the accuracy of weighted biases in approximating weighted averages for a range of LHC data, incorporating various processes and experimental configurations. We find that the PDF-weighted bias is a reliable estimator, with the relative error typically declining below the 1% threshold as the integrated luminosity increases above 100 pb$^{-1}$. We also observe cross-check consistency and anticipate the broad applicability of this finding to additional processes and experimental setups. Furthermore, we utilize our results to suggest optimal luminosity and polarization settings for the next-generation hadron collider that could further reduce theoretical uncertainties. Radio sources with minimal optical counterparts have been of interest for many years and are frequently utilized in radio source selection for wide-field radio observations. Four radio source catalogs were cross-referred to create a comprehensive sample of $10,611$ sources, excluding those with clear optical counterparts. Statistical properties of radio sources with minimal optical counterparts were investigated by categorizing them based on signal-to-noise ratio thresholds in radio data that had been deconvolved for the beam size. Findings indicate that radio sources with minimal optical counterparts exhibit a median signal-to-noise ratio of 5-6 when detected at a threshold of 5$\sigma$. Their characteristic sizes are generally small, typically less than 0.1 arcseconds, with a median size of 0.02 arcseconds. No significant variations in size were found across different signal-to-noise threshold ranges. Analysis of radio source spectra revealed a median spectral index of -0.15, with a wide dispersion of up to 0.25. No significant spectral index changes were found when considering signal-to-noise threshold ranges. Radio power shows a clear correlation with size and spectral index. A sharp cutoff in size and a less pronounced cutoff in spectral index occur at radio powers of around $10^{25}$ W/Hz$^{2}$ in Jy$^2$. All sources with radio powers above this limit have minimal optical counterparts. A relationship between radio power, size, and spectral index can be explained by a combination of radio source orientation and luminosity. A fraction of radio sources with minimal optical counterparts have radio powers indicative of flat radio spectra. A method is proposed to identify hidden narrow radio sources with minimal optical counterparts by analyzing radio data. A hidden radio source population with minimal optical counterparts was discovered in the field of the blazar 3C 111 by analyzing its host galaxy radio spectrum. A similar approach can be applied to numerous blazar fields. It is further recommended that radio follow-up observations be conducted of extragalactic sources identified by wide-field radio surveys, particularly those with minimal optical counterparts in crowded fields. A potential source of contamination in wide-field radio observations of galaxy fields is the presence of radio sources with minimal optical counterparts. It is advisable to account for such sources when estimating total galaxy masses and constructing mass profiles. A small fraction of these sources may also contribute to cosmic ionization. Accurate identification of hidden narrow radio sources with minimal optical counterparts requires radio follow-up of candidates using very long baseline array radio observations. We investigate the instantaneous consequences of a rapid change in momentum on a quantum particle in motion within a classical phonon field, using the Born Oppenheimer approximation as a framework. Within this framework, we identify the minimal description required for phonon states when the particle's momentum varies swiftly. Our study exposes the inherent links between phonon modes and the particle's motion, dictating its spin states. Moreover, we show that fluctuating phonon fields cause the particle's spin to shift constantly, leading to an instantaneous connection between phonon and spin degrees of freedom. Additionally, we quantify the impact on spin coherence and demonstrate the potential for phonon fields to facilitate spin transport. Our results also indicate that phonon-induced perturbations can lead to an imbalance in phonon polarization, potentially being utilized in phonon-based optical phenomena such as phonon polarization switching and phonon nonlinear processes like phonon Rabi splitting. Furthermore, we establish that rapid changes in momentum can trigger phonon oscillations between different states, enabling the production of complex phonons through an electronic driver. Our research lays the foundation for understanding and manipulating the interplay between electron, spin, and phonon states in solid-state systems. We provide theoretical evidence that phonon-induced perturbations can result in the degradation of spin coherence, accompanied by permanent connections between phonon and spin degrees of freedom, leading to the polarization of fluctuating phonon fields, complex phonon generation, and potential solutions to phonon-based optical phenomena. These concepts can be explored in semiconductor quantum dots, organic microcrystals, nitrogen-vacancy centers, and graphene edges using high-intensity optical pulses, with potential applications in quantum information storage, phonon engineering, and photon-phons interactions. Our results demonstrate that momentum-driven phonon and spin fluctuations may offer a means to solve some phantom quantum coherence phenomena and might provide a solution to the challenge of scaling quantum information processing. Additionally, we demonstrate that phonon and spin states can be described using the Born Oppenheimer approximation, a framework initially developed for the study of molecular systems. We anticipate that our findings on the interplay between electron, spin, and phonon states will contribute to a deeper comprehension of quantum phenomena in solid-state systems and will aid in the development of novel quantum technologies. Recent advances in large-language-model-based dialogue have focused on incorporating multimodal information and expansive linguistic skills. However, the semantic diversity of generated text in dialogue has not been adequately addressed. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the Semantic Variety in Dialogue (SeViD) dataset, which includes over 25,000 annotated triples of previous text, current text, and variety scores for 1,000 continuous text continuations. Variety scores indicate the semantic difference between two consecutive texts. To ensure the diversity of generated text, we propose a variety-preserving framework that utilizes natural language inference to guide the selection of diverse options and incorporate variety information into a likelihood estimate. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that this framework leads to a significant increase in semantic variety in generated text continuations. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. Moreover, a method has been developed to identify the minimum number of nodes to split, along with a precise algorithm applying this rule, though it does so with a dependence on an exponential factor exponential to the number of nodes in the smaller group. Furthermore, a more efficient algorithm has been developed for splitting nodes in a bipartite graph, with a time complexity directly proportional to the square of the smaller group's size and the logarithm of the larger group's size. This new approach presents an improvement over prior methods, albeit for simple edge types. The approach has been incorporated into an exact algorithm for identifying the minimum number of nodes to split, leading to a planar drawing following this specific rule. The method has been applied to an important problem within the realm of graph drawing, namely the development of a planar representation for a bipartite graph, where the presence of an edge relies on a specific similarity between nodes in corresponding groups. The approach has been successfully employed in creating a planar representation for a bipartite graph based on the structure of semi-accurate Boolean functions, demonstrating its utility in complex scenarios. The time complexity of the approach has been analyzed in detail, leading to an open question regarding the minimal number of node splits achieved by an optimal solution, even in the case of a small four-node subgroup. The approach has been implemented within a software tool for automating the creation of educational multiple-choice question papers, showcasing its practical applications. The method has been examined in the context of its integration with a user interface, resulting in a user-friendly application following which a planar representation was generated for a set of real-world data, incorporating over a thousand nodes within a bipartite graph. The goal of incremental learning algorithms is to enable machines to adapt to constantly evolving datasets by learning from one batch of data at a time. These models excel at processing large datasets efficiently, especially when the data contains numerous categories. Nevertheless, traditional incremental learning algorithms struggle with mastering new categories, particularly those that are rare or underrepresented. This paper introduces a novel approach, called the Advanced Comparative Analysis of Calibration Methods for Imbalanced Class Incremental Learning, which delves into the comparison of various techniques for maintaining the calibration of models in the face of constantly shifting data with increasingly numerous classes and adapts to the memory constraints of modern computers. This research involves a comprehensive evaluation of 11 different calibration methods and 7 incremental learning algorithms across 7 datasets, resulting in a comprehensive study of the state-of-the-art. This includes a thorough examination of how the selection of algorithm, data, and method for maintaining calibration interacts and affects the performance of the model. This knowledge is critical for developing practical algorithms that can effectively learn from data in real-world applications. This research also yields a suite of versatile experiments that facilitate the assessment of pre-trained models in class incremental learning scenarios. In order to produce highly accurate and versatile deep neural network (DNN) models, today's AI-powered applications typically require significant computational resources and energy consumption. Due to the proliferation of DNNs across mobile devices and cloud platforms, achieving high performance computing and efficient energy usage has become a top priority. System designers use a technique called precision tuning to balance performance and efficiency, where they exploit the degradation in model accuracy that results from increasing the bit precision of floating-point computations. However, this approach reaches a limit as further increases in precision yield minimal reductions in accuracy, making it ineffective. To overcome this limitation, we introduce HyperDegrade, a novel technique that utilizes simultaneous multi-precision execution on a single central processing unit (CPU) to achieve improved performance and energy efficiency. Through 15 distinct deep neural network benchmarks across multiple applications and across various CUs, we demonstrate that HyperDegrade can attain average performance gains of 4.5 times and average energy reductions of 5.6 times when comparing 16-bit computations to 11-bit computations. Furthermore, HyperDegrade can attain average accuracy losses of 0.053% and 0.064% for floating-point and fixed-point computations, respectively. With its simplicity and flexibility, HyperDegrade provides an enhanced precision tuning framework that can be applied to various computing platforms. To facilitate widespread adoption of DNNs across all computing devices, we recommend the development of DNN models that utilize fixed-point arithmetic, as these can be seamlessly optimized across different precision levels. With this approach, HyperDegrade can be used to design more energy-efficient and performance-driven DNN applications that can run seamlessly on any computing platform. Through our research, we have created an automated tool that can convert and optimize a wide range of deep learning frameworks that support fixed-point arithmetic. We have also introduced a novel method for identifying optimal conversion thresholds that can be used across multiple applications and CUs. All of our research, including our techniques and our benchmarking platform, has been thoroughly evaluated and the results of our studies have been included in our findings. Due to its unique combination of high performance and low energy consumption, HyperDegrade has the potential to serve as a robust framework for developing a wide range of deep learning applications that can run efficiently and effectively on any computing platform. Since this new particle likely interacts strongly with the Higgs, it is likely that the Higgs dominates its decay into di-muon. Typically, surgeons rely on pre-operative planning and a thorough understanding of the patient's anatomy. However, in cases of complex congenital heart diseases, the arrangement of heart structures can be difficult to navigate using just medical images. Our study explored whether a U-Net-based segmentation network, trained on a large dataset of normal and abnormal heart structures from high-resolution magnetic resonance images, could accurately identify specific heart areas in patients with rare congenital heart diseases. We analyzed the results of two independent sets of data and found that the model performed well on both, with a high score of 0.93 in terms of Dice similarity coefficient. Interestingly, the model's performance wasn't significantly impacted by the presence of cardiac malformations it wasn't designed for, indicating a high potential for its use in treating a broad spectrum of congenital heart diseases. However, the study also highlighted the challenges associated with training a precise model using a large dataset, despite the availability of advanced computing power. To achieve this, we had to combine two independent datasets, which resulted in a combined dataset of 6000 images, which was subsequently split into two parts - a training set of 4800 images and a validation set of 1200 images. This issue is exacerbated in complex scenes with diverse objects. To address this limitation, a novel approach called Universal Detection (UD) has been proposed, aiming to enhance the robustness of object detection by modeling all objects within the dataset as potential targets. This approach is framed within a multi-task framework that simultaneously performs both universal detection and classification. To validate the UD approach, a comprehensive dataset called the Universal Detection Dataset (UDD) needs to be created through careful selection of datasets that encompass a wide range of categories and are minimally overlapping in terms of training and evaluation images. This is achieved here by combining the PASCAL VOC dataset with OpenImages, leading to the creation of the minimal UDD dataset consisting of 21 classes. This new dataset is further expanded into the full UDD containing 5,011 classes before applying clustering to define the final object categories for the dataset. This results in 4,523 distinct objects in the UDD dataset. To evaluate the UD approach, a new evaluation metric called the Universal Detection Accuracy (UDA) is introduced, reporting a significant performance improvement of +5.2% over the baseline method when applied to the minimal UDD dataset. This gain is consistent across multiple evaluation settings and implies that models optimized for UDA tend to exhibit better class-agnostic performance. To achieve these gains, a new model architecture called the Universal Detection Network (UDN) is introduced, incorporating additional convolutional layers and achieving better results than the baseline model. This is further validated by applying the UDN architecture to the full UDD dataset, resulting in a 6.5% improvement in UDA. To facilitate the training of models for the UD task, a distance-based sampling approach is proposed to reduce the over-representation of easily detected objects in the dataset. This method enables models to focus on more challenging objects and produce a more balanced training dataset. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require combining various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a mix of written text and visual elements, as seen in guidebooks that contain ordered steps for completing tasks. The availability of multimodal guidebooks on the web enables us to study procedural knowledge in a data-driven manner. Current approaches focus on individual modalities, using natural language processing or computer vision to analyze written descriptions and images, respectively. In contrast, multimodal sequential models offer a more comprehensive understanding of these data. However, there is a significant gap in the current research literature, with no study having yet attempted to incorporate the diverse forms of information found in real-world procedural datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Multimodal Procedural Knowledge Benchmark, which comprises a dataset of ordered steps communicated through a combination of text and images and is accompanied by a suite of sequential multimodal models designed to evaluate the various aspects of procedural knowledge. The performance of these models is then assessed on their ability to understand the sequence of events, the relationships between events, and the relevance of each step to the overall procedure. Our findings indicate that incorporating the interdependencies between modalities and using more sophisticated models of sequential processing leads to significant improvements in accurately sequencing unordered events and accurately identifying the components of a procedure. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, the sloshing Sagnac design can be implemented using existing laser interferometer gravitational wave detectors with mirror modifications, and its parameters are adaptable to different detector configurations. The concept has been theoretically explored and simulated with COMPUTE and the LIGO Software Suite. The results indicate that this novel design can significantly enhance the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors in the high-frequency range. The model predicts a 20-30% improvement in detection sensitivity at 500 Hz, and up to a 50% enhancement at 1000 Hz for certain binary neutron star merger events. The detection of gravitational waves produced by binary neutron star mergers such as GW170608 could be achieved with a 10-20% improvement in sensitivity at 450 Hz. The design offers improved signal-to-noise ratios of up to 20%, which could be beneficial for identifying new gravitational wave events. The results also suggest that the sloshing Sagnac design can provide a 5-10% better match to simulated binary neutron star merger waveforms in search algorithms. The design's performance is on par with the upgraded signal-recycled Michelson detector that employs quantum entangled sources, and it represents a viable option for upgrading current gravitational wave detectors with better quantum efficiency photodetectors. The model predicts that the new design will be capable of identifying events like GW170608 at frequencies up to 450 Hz. The design's ability to detect gravitational waves in the 400-700 Hz range could be enhanced by improving the power recycled ratio, which would allow it to identify events like GW170608 at these frequencies with a 10-20% better signal-to-noise ratio. Despite initial intuition that a simple 3-band d-only model would suffice, our study shows that this assumption is too limited. Instead, we find that the complexity of transition metal oxides often demands a more intricate model, incorporating both d and p correlated states. Utilizing the FT-DFT+DMFT method, we derived the real-frequency spectrum of SrMnO$_3$, demonstrating how the complexity of these materials can be effectively unraveled through a detailed analysis of spectral functions. Our results reveal subtle p-d coupling effects and clarify the distinction between correlated states and molecular effective energies within the Wannier representation. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces from two-dimensional images is a difficult image processing problem due to possible disruptions from, for example, occlusions or if one face is heavily obscured by another. This challenging issue is compounded by the complexity of the Haar wavelet representation used to represent faces in this process. One common approach to handling such complexities within a deep neural network is to employ a regression-based technique, combining training data with representations that are less complex than Haar wavelets. The conventional method within this approach involves training a single network to predict the entire face representation at once, which can result in overfitting and significantly impede the detection and accommodation of distortions. To address this limitation, we propose modifying the regression-based deep learning approach as follows: first, divide the face representation into more manageable parts; second, employ two separate networks to predict these component parts independently; third, incorporate a self-alignment mechanism that ensures the accuracy of each prediction by drawing on the output from the other network; and fourth, utilize both the predicted representations and the network outputs to correct any discrepancies. This enhanced method was successfully applied to the 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction task in the widely used CASPEAL database. Our results demonstrate that our proposed method not only outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques but also achieves very satisfactory performance without relying on metadata, which is commonly required for initialization purposes. Moreover, this method's resilience to facial distortions was validated through a newly introduced evaluation metric called the residual average diameter ratio (SADR), which indicates that our proposed method yields consistent performance across all difficulty levels. This method's effectiveness is further confirmed by a visual comparison of the reconstructed faces in both the training and testing phases. Moreover, a paper award was given to this work at the 2021 International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV). In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the importance of understanding how models generalize across similar time series data sets. This study explores a time series linear model with an over-parameterized network and extensive data sets, finding that overfitting is a prevalent phenomenon despite its named danger. Our research demonstrates that, interestingly, increasing the model's complexity does not necessarily lead to inaccurate predictions and, under certain conditions, precise ones. A theoretical analysis and a comprehensive algorithm for drawing unbiased samples from the time series linear model distribution have been developed to further study its properties. Our experiments show that overfitting occurs commonly, yet somehow the models' performance does not suffer, and sometimes even improves, as we increase the number of parameters. This is visually represented with a performance landscape, showing that, counterintively, the generalization error can increase while the training error decreases, and vice versa. Our research also introduces a new perspective on how the models generalize across similar time series data sets, depending on the models' and data sets' characteristics. Our results suggest that overfitting leads to better performance in these situations and, interestingly, that it happens more frequently when the data sets have a higher variance. Our research implies that, interestingly, overparameterization might already be optimal, and that further research is needed to fully understand these phenomena. Our public code and the time series linear model distribution samples generator are publicly available at https://github.com/marcomamino/benign_overfitting. However, there is a significant gap between the technology and its application due to the poor image quality and varied nature of x-ray images, resulting in limited and lower image resolution datasets available for training. In this study, we introduce a new high-quality benchmark containing 10 categories of prohibited items, along with 200,000 high-resolution images at 5 different scales, based on the MIO dataset. To enhance the accuracy of detection on low-resolution x-ray images, we designed a lateral inhibition module that emulates human visual system's scaling strategy. This includes a module that up-scales low-resolution images to their original size and extracts features at multiple scales, followed by a module that integrates the feature maps with different scales and reduces noise with a lateral inhibition mechanism. In experiments, our proposed method demonstrated superior performance on both the MIO and PFD100K benchmarks, achieving a mean average precision (mAP) of 43.51% on the MIO dataset and significantly outperforming existing prosthetic network methods. Additionally, our method showed great potential in applying deep learning to real-world x-ray security examination. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to incorporate contextual information and glosses found in on-line dictionaries to enhance the performance of WSD tasks.  However, the limitations of these approaches have also become apparent, primarily due to the reliance on a single context and a single gloss for each word sense.  To address this issue, a new context-gloss network is proposed that utilizes multiple contexts and glosses associated with a word sense to facilitate the learning of a word's sense representation.  The proposed network is then integrated with an attention-based mechanism to combine the word's intrinsic properties with its context and gloss features.  Experimental results indicate that the proposed method yields superior performance when compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches, according to evaluations conducted on the WordSense Embedding Evaluation Framework.  Furthermore, the proposed method is found to generate a more robust and distributive word sense representation when compared to other techniques.  The integrated attention-based method is found to be particularly effective at disambiguating polysemous words even when the context and gloss are inconsistent, thereby exhibiting the ability to capture a word's sense invariant properties.  The proposed context-gloss network architecture is also discovered to yield a word sense representation that correlates well with the definitions provided in on-line dictionaries, thereby demonstrating its practical applications. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma during the EDA phase require further study. A survey of previously identified PTMs reveals they appear in plasmas with edge currents exceeding the critical stability threshold and featuring active edge pedicles. A numerical model based on the edge plasma response is developed and successfully replicates the PTM at the JET-like conditions, contradicting previous beliefs that the model's limitations would prevent it from capturing the phenomenon. A distinct feature of the model, characterized as a "polar edge pedestal," emerges and is shown to result from the model's incorporation of a thin magnetic flux layer at the edge, producing a distinct pedestal structure. This discovery implies that the PTM's underlying cause lies in the interaction between the external magnetic field and the responding plasma, rather than an intrinsic instability in the plasma itself. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in organized ways, but the following issues persist: most methods require individual expert evaluations of a substantial number of configurations; the models they use often lack a clear physical interpretation and may not account for real-world restrictions on system configurations. To address these challenges, we present BoGraph, a new approach that utilizes graph-structured data representing acceptable system configurations and their performances. By creating a kernel density estimate (KDE) based on previously collected data, BoGraph identifies configurations to test next. It achieves this by incorporating real-world constraint information into a suitability score, thus making it possible to organize the search for optimal system configurations by their feasibility. We applied BoGPU, a variant of BoGraph, to the challenge of optimizing a high-performance GPU implementation for sorting. The results showed that it outperforms an unstructured Bayesian optimization method while respecting real-world configuration constraints. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a difficult aspect of three-dimensional object detection. The difficulty arises because distant objects appear tiny in images, making it challenging to obtain precise density predictions. Furthermore, the limited spatial coverage means that the spatial attention mechanism is not effectively activated for distant objects, hindering the ability to obtain precise size and class predictions. The problem is compounded by the fact that real-world datasets do not provide labels for objects at far-field distances, making it difficult to evaluate the performance of three-dimensional object detection models. The Far3D metric is proposed to address this issue by providing a unified framework that incorporates both precision and recall rates for evaluating three-dimensional object detection models at far-field distances. An analysis of the proposed metric is conducted through both theoretical and experimental approaches, leading to the creation of the Far3Det benchmark to serve as a challenging evaluation protocol for model evaluation. The code for the benchmark can be found at https://github.com/linge-xu/Far3Det, and the benchmark has been incorporated into the MMDet framework at https://gitee.com/mmdet/mmdet/commit/0e2a5d3c8b1a2f2a8a7d2f3e4f5f6f7. Top-performing models for the Far3Det benchmark can be found at https://github.com/linge-xu/Far3Det/commit/0e2a5d3c8b1a2f2a8a7d2f3e4f5f6f7. The far-field three-dimensional identification task has been successfully demonstrated through both theoretical and experimental approaches, leading to the discovery of a phenomenon termed "density gap" which indicates that the density of three-dimensional objects decreases at a rate of $1/\sqrt r$ as the distance $r$ increases, providing insights that can be applied to the design of models for far-field three-dimensional identification. The achieved state-of-the-art performance on the Far3Det benchmark confirms the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The study of far-field three-dimensional identification is also extended to low-light conditions, leading to the creation of the near-field three-dimensional identification task. The code for the study can be found at https://github.com/linge-xu/Far3Det. The profound impact of the study on the field of three-dimensional object detection is presented in the conclusion. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, estimating scene flow is complicated due to the necessity of accurately measuring displacement between points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Traditional approaches primarily use conventional maximization problems including maximum likelihood estimation and rank minimization, though these methods fail to consider fundamental metrics properties. Intuitively, a suitable metric should conform to the collectible and co-variance principles. Although previous works attempted to learn scene flow estimators through self-supervision, they overlooked the impact of undesirable measurements on the algorithm's performance. Moreover, the assumption that accurate measurements are collected for training and validation is unrealistic. The proposed Adversarial Metric Learning framework acknowledges the presence of noisy measurements during data collection. It includes a novel metric learning component that treats unknown scene flow as latent points, utilizing pairwise constraints to identify undesirable measurements. The framework further incorporates a multi-view feature learning component that utilizes unknown scene flow points to extract motion-orientated features from RGB images. The Adversarial Metric Learning framework includes a context-encouraging component that integrates the learned features and unknown scene flow points to estimate scene flow via non-local mutual restriction. The framework is entirely self-supervised and enables the estimation of scene flow based on collected and noisy measurements. Comprehensive experiments validate the efficacy of the Adversarial Metric Learning framework, showcasing superior scene flow estimation results in comparison to state-of-the-art self-supervised and supervised approaches. The project's code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/Adversarial-Metric-Learning-for-Scene-Flow. The experiment conducted demonstrates the algorithm's capability to estimate scene flow in real-time, with approximately 30 milliseconds per frame. Furthermore, the model's accuracy was found to correlate with the proportion of noisy measurements incorporated. A model incorporating 20% noisy measurements achieved a mean flow error of 6.93, whereas a model with 0% noisy measurements achieved a mean flow error of 5.93. This paper introduces a novel approach called Timeloops, which allows for the automated generation of system call policies for containerized microservices. By leveraging static analysis and profiling, Timeloops creates a temporal policy learning framework that can generate policies to govern the execution of a program within a specific time frame. This framework is the basis for an efficient and scalable system call policy evaluation process, which incorporates a minimal set of temporal pointers. We demonstrate the efficacy of Timeloops by applying it to a real-world use case and showcasing its capacity for across-genre generalization. Our approach results in substantial performance improvements, with system call overhead reduced to a minimum. Additionally, Timeloops offers transparent and manageable policy management, thereby providing a seamless user experience. The source code and experimental setup of this study are now available on GitHub. With the advent of cloud computing and software-as-a-service, software security has become increasingly dependent on system call policies, which is, in turn, fueling the growth of search for compositional non-interference and related techniques. Recently, a novel feature was introduced in transmission electron microscopes, allowing for the adjustment of electron optical system performance through a programmable phase plate. This development has sparked interest in the research community, and several proposed designs for such a feature have been showcased. However, the underlying physics underlying these designs remains poorly understood, leading to misconceptions about their potential to correct for spherical aberration. This commentary aims to illuminate the fundamental physics behind these designs, revealing the unseen distortions they introduce and the inherent limitations of programming a phase plate to achieve desired electron optical properties. Furthermore, we highlight the superiority of liquid cell phase plates, and the potential for programmable solid state phase plates to serve a more appropriate functional purpose, that of mimicking astigmatism, a phenomenon the research community has thus far overlooked. We anticipate this commentary to shed new light on the subject, providing a basis for informed discussion and guidance for future research in this area. Additionally, we suggest a method for experimentally validating the capabilities of programmable phase plates, and we outline a conceptual design for a new type of electron optical system that incorporates a programmable solid state phase plate, presenting an opportunity for community members to contribute through shared goals and a common metric. This development has the potential to address the ongoing challenges faced by electron microscopy practitioners in obtaining consistent results, and it may also pave the way for a renewed focus on electron optical system design, facilitated by advancements in computational modeling, 3D printing technology, and the incorporation of novel materials. Nonetheless, a resolution to the long-standing issue of spherical aberration in electron microscopy appears to be a solution for an electron optical system problem that has been effectively managed through the use of electron lenses with negative focal length, a design that has become standard practice over five decades ago. Nonetheless, this commentary is intended to provide a platform for the exchange of ideas, and it is hoped that it may inspire a community response that could address a pressing concern for the electron microscopy community. The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain information necessary for sound text generation may not be adequately captured by these encoder representations, which is corroborated by additional analysis conducted on pre-trained models. As a result, we introduce a method for augmenting the training of these models to improve the richness of the representations they employ, leading to enhanced performance across various evaluation metrics and models. Our implementations and data are freely accessible at https://github.com/TharashD/Do-Encodings-Matter. While significant progress has been made in developing data-driven dialogue models, several critical aspects continue to be explored, and this work addresses a fundamental question encompassing all of these topics: What underlying understanding must a model possess to excel in generating text for real-world conversations? Nonetheless, the answers to this inquiry will inevitably evolve as the field of conversational understanding continues to mature and shift. As such, we strongly believe that researchers and practitioners should remain open to adjusting their methodologies in accordance with the emerging benchmarks and methods for evaluating models of this type. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Additionally, we investigated the screening of an external electric field by the Dirac electrons in doped graphene and found that the resulting electric field distribution changes from circular at very low temperatures to roughly triangular as temperature increases. This study provides a theoretical framework for experimenting on doped graphene and understanding the influence of temperature and screening on observed phenomena. Furthermore, the developed model can be adapted to study other two-dimensional Dirac materials. In the case of half-filled graphene, we found that the screening fails due to anti-alignment of the spins of Dirac electrons. Consequently, a external electric field induces an intrinsic polarization in this material, with the resulting polarization increasing with temperature. This phenomenon is expected to occur in other half-filled tight-binding models featuring Dirac electrons. In the case of graphene, the failure of screening allows the resonance of the external electric field with the formation of a zero-energy surface state, which results in unusual angular dependence of the thermal capacity and a prominent peak in the thermal capacity when the doping concentration moves from the valence band to the conductance band. This phenomenon is expected to occur in other low-energy systems described by a relativistic effective theory. Additionally, we found that the thermal screening can drive a phase transition in doped graphene from a half-filled situation, with the resulting change in the thermal capacity displaying an exponential dependence on temperature. This explanation for the screening-induced phase transition provides a clear understanding of his phenomenon and predicts the critical properties of the phase transition. This knowledge can be applied to experimentally identify the phase transition by measuring the thermal capacity or compressibility of doped graphene at low temperatures and varying the doping concentration carefully.
