The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra than their non-asynchronous counterparts. 

Using complete samples of non-asynchronous and asynchronous polars from the 3rd ROSAT survey, we performed a statistical analysis of their X-ray hardness ratios. Our data show that asynchronous polars have a more intense X-ray spectrum than non-asynchronous polars, in agreement with prior research. Moreover, we discovered that this difference becomes more pronounced at lower flux levels, a phenomenon that might be attributed to the greater accuracy of binary alignment in asynchronous polars or the presence of accretion in some systems. 

However, when dividing the samples based on accretion indicators rather than synchronization status, we found that a greater proportion of non-synchronized systems are identified as X-ray brightest, whereas the majority of accretors are synchronized. As a result, the greater detection rate of non-synchronized systems in soft gamma-ray surveys can be attributed to a combination of a more intense X-ray spectrum and a higher accretion rate rather than binary alignment. Our study's outcomes have implications for future X-ray surveys, specifically the enhanced sensitivity of eROSITA, which is likely to significantly enhance the detection rate of asynchronous polars. 
Finally, we note that the absence of spin period variability in the X-ray spectrum of the solitary accretor V1466 Aql, which shares characteristics with asynchronous polars, implies that this effect might be related to the presence of the companion star's gravitational influence on the white dwarf's spin period. 
Additionally, we provide reasons to believe that the solitary accretor GD1618 might also exhibit the binary characteristics of an asynchronous polar, while its variable spin period, coupled with its enhanced X-ray spectrum, suggests it may be an object in a stage of binary evolution where the white dwarf's spin period is no longer synchronized with the binary orbital period.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. Code is available at https://github.com/ChihYu Chen/FourierMask.

This study seeks to establish criteria for the range of functions that map one dimensionless space onto another dimensionless space, specifically within the context of Euclidean geometry. A pair of functions f and g are defined as intimately connected if their composition g followed by composition f results in the same outcome as the composition f followed by composition g. In mathematical terms, this is expressed as g o f = f o g. A significant aspect of connected functions is their shared trajectory or range. Music education on head-mounted virtual reality (VMR) devices has not been extensively explored, likely due to the limited understanding of their potential as engaging educational tools. Despite advancements in technology, there is a noticeable lack of compositions generated through VR music education that surpass basic musical notes played in unison. We believe this setback arises from the restrictive nature of traditional educational approaches used in VR settings. To overcome this, we present a novel, award-winning VR music education platform called Pied Piper, designed for the Meta Quest. By emphasizing creativity and interactive learning, Pied Piper encourages users to explore a wide range of musical genres while developing their harmonic and melodic skills. What's remarkable about Pied Piper is that it has produced several notable musical compositions, including ones that have charted on Billboard, highlighting the effectiveness of its compositional methodology. Our study with over 150 participants across three experiments demonstrates the efficacy of Pied Piper in teaching music through a self-directed, engaging VR experience. Our analysis of user data reveals the platform's capability to monitor a user's musical progress, identify areas of improvement, and provide personalized advice. To showcase the versatility of VR music education, we also present a case study on adapting Pied Piper for use in therapeutic settings with individuals struggling with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). To facilitate further research and development in VR music education, we openly share our dataset, methodologies, and the Pied Piper protocol. Our work paves the way for the exploration of complex musical concepts, multi-instrument compositions, and personalized music education in VR environments. Additionally, we highlight several technical challenges that currently impede the development of seamless VR music education experiences and present a high-level architecture for addressing these issues. This architecture can serve as a reference point for designing more sophisticated VR music education platforms that can deliver a broad range of musical education, from basic note playing to advanced musical analysis and composition. Our study also highlights the need for the development of more intuitive VR music input methods that can accurately capture the nuances of human performance. To contribute to the advancement of this field, we present a novel VR music input protocol called the Pied Piper Protocol, along with a prototype of a more expressive VR music controller called the Pied Piper Controller. This prototype can detect complex musical directions and has demonstrated its effectiveness in conjunction with the Pied Piper platform. We believe that the combination of advanced VR music processing, more expressive VR controllers, and self-directed learning protocols such as the Pied Piper algorithm will revolutionize the way music is learned and composed in the future. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECR arrivals with high-energy neutrino detections, as neutrinos point directly to their sources without being affected by neutrino interactions. This paper presents the results of a historical neutrino search, conducted between 2010 and 2018, with all detected neutrinos serving as potential UHECR neutrino sources. It identifies nine high-energy neutrino events that could be associated with UHECR arrival directions containing more than $10^{10}$ GeV of energy, resulting in four significant spatial patterns at the $4.5\%$ confidence level, which could be linked to massive star formations, radio binaries, and pulsar alignments, or might be entirely random. Additionally, three areas with a $3.2\%$ confidence level for multiple UHECR arrivals and high-energy neutrino detections were found, with one such instance displaying characteristics similar to supernovae remnant directions. Furthermore, no significant correlations were found with other potential sources of UHECR, such as black holes, supermassive black holes, and the Sun, or during solar flare and cosmic ray acceleration events. This discovery, or lack thereof, sets the stage for future analyses with an expanded neutrino dataset. With that, we outline a strategy to execute a more in-depth examination of spatial relationships between high-energy neutrinos and UHECRs. This protocol can serve as a method for identifying significant correlations between these cosmic rays and neutrinos, encompassing multivariate contexts, which would be invaluable for the next generation of neutrino and UHECR facilities. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.  Our study used a multimodal approach that combined verbal and non-verbal data to improve the validity of our results and provided a detailed analysis of our automated detection method for identifying curiosity in real-time.  Finally, our study established a foundation for investigating curiosity in a wide range of learning environments and identified key variables that affect curiosity in small group settings. Deep learning-based automated emergency response systems and related services like Siri, Google Assistant, and Alexa have become ubiquitous in modern life, offering quick assistance in life-threatening situations. Nonetheless, numerous incidents have highlighted the critical weakness of these systems, which rely heavily on cultural and ethical principles, but are designed with little consideration for such aspects. Our research reveals that current deep learning models used in these systems are prone to extreme reactions and persistent inaccuracy when faced with sensitive issues like racial and gender biases, resulting in ineffective responses to critical situations. To address this problem, we propose an innovative framework that combines word-based semantics and syntax to explain the inconsistencies in these systems' outputs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method to identify instances of inequitable treatment and suggest a framework for incorporating diverse perspectives into the development of these systems. Our proposed approach was applied to a dataset of emergency scenarios, demonstrating its capability to achieve better performance and reduce bias. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus identification algorithm capable of accurately detecting and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus identification in pathology images. In contrast to conventional models that only focus on capturing spatial and local characteristics, this network leverages a unique structure that simultaneously considers both coarse and fine details of the image. By utilizing two parallel branches, it explicitly extracts both global and local information, thereby enhancing the quality of the mapping between image features and nucleus targets. To support the rigorous evaluation of the proposed method, a larger, more comprehensive dataset was created by combining existing collections of cancer cell images. Experimental results indicate that the W-shaped network Leverages a comprehensive dataset to achieve superior performance, obtaining outstanding accuracy and segmentation quality on a vast dataset of 104,000 images. A particularly noteworthy aspect of this research is the demonstration of the network's capability to reduce dataset dependence, showcasing its potential to solve complex real-world image analysis challenges. A key contribution of this study is the availability of a wide range of models optimized for nucleus target in pathology images, enabling the exploration of their relative strengths and weaknesses. A further contribution is the examination of the effect of overfitting on the target of the network, along with the presentation of the optimal model for large-scale datasets, along with a comprehensive evaluation of the W-shaped network against a suite of state-of-the-art baselines. A key limitation of this study is the lack of experimental validation on real-world cancer diagnosis scenarios, a key area for further research. A further contribution is the exploration of the potential of the W-shaped network to solve other demanding image segmentation tasks, along with a discussion of its potential applications in cancer diagnosis facilitated by deep learning. A further contribution is the release of the comprehensive dataset created for the evaluation of the proposed method, alongside the optimal models trained thereon.

This paper investigates the relationship between L^k(G) and G's hamiltonian path index (HPI). Specifically, if L^k(G) has a hamiltonian path, the question arises as to whether this property can be inherited by L^(k-1)(G), L^(k-2)(G), and so on, until we reach G itself. This paper provides a counterexample to demonstrate that the property of having a hamiltonian path cannot be consistently inherited across the sequence of repeated line graphs. Nevertheless, it is proven that if L^k(G) is a hamiltonian graph, then G itself will also be a hamiltonian graph, though this condition cannot be extrapolated to an infinite series of line graphs. Additionally, the problem of determining whether the property of having a hamiltonian path can be inherited by a connected graph after applying the operation of creating a line graph exactly k times presents an open question. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory treatments, resulting in potential benefits for patients with COVID-19. Furthermore, we discuss the model's applicability and the scope for its expansion to explore more intricate cellular systems. Ultimately, our work highlights the value of incorporating biological detail into cellular models and the potential for using such models to identify treatment targets in the context of COVID-19.

This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the impact of these variables on the reward signal is established, resulting in a simplified environment that can be used for policy evaluation and value function estimation. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring regular-dose CT images from low-dose images, yielding restoration results very close to those achieved using supervised learning. However, the use of two neural networks (the generator and the reverse generator) as well as two unsupervised learning processes (training on both low-dose to regular-dose CT and regular-dose to low-dose CT datasets) significantly increases the computational requirements. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new cycleGAN architecture based on a single AdaIN-switchable network. By utilizing AdaIN switches to switch between two operations and allowing unshared learned mappings in the reverse process, our model greatly simplifies the architecture while still allowing for accurate restoration of CT images. Comprehensive evaluations using four public CT datasets demonstrate that our method not only matches the performance of traditional cycleGANs but also achieves comparable results to a state-of-the-art supervised learning network, all while reducing the number of parameters by a significant margin. Furthermore, we apply our method to a real-world low-dose CT reconstruction problem involving hippocampal image enhancement, obtaining visually pleasing results that outperform existing techniques. Overall, our efficient AdaIN-switchable cycleGAN opens up new avenues for the practical application of cycleGANs in clinical CT image enhancement tasks. Additionally, our code is publicly available on https://github.com/AlvinHuang3/AdaIN-Switch-cycleGAN. To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method onto the deformed wave functions of single-particle potentials and applied this to well-known $^{20}$Ne, $^{68}$Zn, and $^{68}$Ni nuclei. Our self-consistent deformed potentials were derived from the Skyrme-Hartree-Fock method. Rotational shape decoupling effects were examined by comparing the total binding energies of these nuclei after angular momentum projection with the energies of their self-consistent deformed ground states. Our findings indicate that rotational shape decoupling can accurately explain the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei and suggest that their rotational characteristics may be understood through the involvement of high-$l$ orbital angular momentum components, consistent with the definition of distorted halo nuclei. Moreover, our study implies that rotational shape decoupling can be applicable not only to ground states but also to excited states in the context of nuclear physics. Additionally, we analyzed the rotational shape decoupling effects in $N$=$Z$ and near-$N$=$Z$ nuclei, finding that the angular momentum projection method can restore $SU(4)$ symmetry, which is broken in the self-consistent deformed potentials. Furthermore, our study highlights the significance of experimental data on transitional states between ground and collective states in distorted halo nuclei. Lastly, we propose potential applications of rotational shape decoupling effects in physics beyond the standard model by utilizing nuclear rotational states as a probe of the existence of extra spatial dimensions or the variation of fundamental parameters with the location. Additionally, we explore the possibility of rotational shape decoupling being a hallmark of quantum chaos in nuclear physics. A descriptive representation of the rotational state of a distorted halo nucleus is provided through a quantum chaos indicator, and the complex deformed potential of these nuclei may be regarded as a manifestation of quantum chaos that gives rise to the irreversible increase in binding energy with the angular momentum in nuclear physics. Lastly, we examine the rotational state of a distorted halo nucleus at its ground state using the matrix product operators, incorporating the concept of quantum entropy in the study of quantum systems, and propose that the rotational state of these nuclei may serve as a model for studying quantum entropy in nuclear physics. Additionally, we outline the theoretical framework for investigating rotational shape decoupling effects in nuclear physics through electronic excitation spectra in the study of quantum systems, and we suggest that the rotational state of distorted halo nuclei may serve as a model for researching the concepts of wave function localization and quantum phase space in nuclear physics.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we present an enhanced version, BasicVSR++, which addresses several limitations of the original formulation. Specifically, we recognize that the original dark channel calculation is flawed and instead use an alternative method, along with a different deformation-based alignment technique. Additionally, we find that the original feature alignment step can introduce noise, which we rectify by integrating a feature alignment regularization mechanism. The interstellar medium (ISM) contains structures that affect radio signals from distant pulsars, often revealing the characteristics of the ISM. These structures, or "scintillation patterns," can be mapped to determine the path of the radio signals and the composition of the ISM. In a study of the bright pulsar B1133+16, researchers discovered a detailed "fingerprint" of the line-of-sight, which they call a "regional scintillation pattern." This pattern is narrow, at approximately 0.5 km/s, and the study finds that it is not as complex as those surrounding other pulsars. Additionally, the pattern shows evidence of magnetic field alignment, following a direction perpendicular to the plane of the pulsar's motion. The study finds that the scintillation pattern is not consistent with Earth-based observations of the surrounding environment, indicating the presence of an unseen feature somewhere between 5 and 25 parsecs from the Sun. The study also presents multiple variations of the scintillation pattern, identified as "sidebands," which occur at specific frequencies corresponding to the "carrier modulation sideband" phenomenon. The study finds that these sidebands are caused by additional structures in the line-of-sight, which are aligned with the plane of the pulsar's motion. The study also presents a 3D map of the surrounding environment based on the "sideband structure," which is a detailed representation of the structures affecting radio signals from the pulsar. Unlike previously studied type 3.02 meteorites Adams (2007) and Graves (2010), these new samples exhibited higher water content and deuterium-to-hydrogen ratios. This led us to consider the possibility that the parent body experienced a partial dehydration process during its accretion stage. By modeling this process, we found the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratios to be 3-4 times higher in the Benenitra pyroxene and up to 5.5 times higher in the Chelyabinsk pyroxene. These enhanced ratios cannot be explained by subsequent alterations and must have originated from the partial dehydration of the planetesimals during the accretion of the solar system's inner portion. Our model indicates that the water content in these particles was reduced to less than 0.4% by weight and deuterium-to-hydrogen ratios reached 1.5 times the solar value. This outcome aligns with the idea that a dust layer with high water content and deuterium enrichment, resulting from the condensation of a solar-composition gas, could have experienced a degree of re-circulation during the accretion process, thus being re-melted and re-solidified at a temperature of approximately 1050 Kelvin. This 'damp dust' layer is believed to have contributed to the formation of the Earth and other terrestrial planets. Our research provides new evidence and supports the theory that the inner solar system planetesimals experienced a degree of re-melting due to accretional heat, with implications for the origin and diversity of terrestrial planets. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of further studying type 3.0 meteorites like Chelyabinsk and Benenitra, which are now recognized as representing a more 'damp' variant of the typical type 3 meteorites, and suggests that their parent bodies might have lost their largest crustal segments as a result of impact events, whereas the remaining smaller craters retained 'damp' crustal reservoirs with deuterium-enriched water, as seen in the type 3.02 meteorites Adams (2007) and Graves (2010). This study also offers a theoretical framework that could be applied to better comprehend the formation of the Earth and other terrestrial planets

This concept has been demonstrated through an experimental model, which was trained on a large public dataset and tested on another large dataset with varying lung conditions. The results showed that existing GAN-based models are not yet fully developed for enhancing medical images and suggested several challenges and potential improvements. Furthermore, a quantitative evaluation of current GAN-based models was conducted, highlighting the difficulties associated with noise in medical images and the limitations of current evaluation metrics. Finally, to address these challenges, a new metric was introduced, along with modifications to pre-training and batch normalization that could lead to further advancements in this field. This work has the potential to contribute to the development of more accurate lung disease diagnosis models and provides a starting point for exploring the editing of lung images in-depth. This is particularly significant because lung diseases are often diagnosed primarily through the interpretation of chest X-ray images, and the introduction of artificial intelligence-based models that can accurately identify and treat diseases from images will inevitably lead to a higher demand for high-quality training data. This need poses these three primary research questions: How can noise in medical images be reduced? Can the performance of GAN-based models be enhanced? And what further advancements can be made in the deployment of deep learning-based models in a practice-oriented setting? These research objectives are the foundation for several potential exploration paths outlined in this work.
